Main Points
⏺ Wallets usually connect through RPC nodes instead of reading the chain themselves
⏺ Node quality affects speed, reliability, and data accuracy
⏺ This post explains why “the network is lagging” can actually mean infrastructure trouble

1️⃣ What It Is — an RPC node handles wallet/app requests: balances, history, and transaction submission.
2️⃣ Why It Exists — most users don’t run full nodes, so interfaces rely on external infrastructure.
3️⃣ Risk Surface — nodes can lag, fail, filter data, or return incomplete results.
4️⃣ Privacy Angle — node providers may see which addresses and IPs are making requests.
5️⃣ Practical Rule — use reliable providers, switch endpoints during issues, and verify important data in explorers.

Final Thoughts

An RPC node is the bridge between your wallet and the chain. If that bridge is weak, the blockchain may be fine while your experience breaks.

posts.text:
Something I realize more and more, with trading but also with life, is that not everything is under our control, and that more is not necessarily better.

For example, I've been bullish since January/February, when price reached the expected main support zone of $60k-70k:

[https://t.me/CryptoCapoTG_Official/1004], [https://x.com/CryptoCapo_/status/2019434869001195948?s=20]

Since then, 5 months have passed by, which is a lot of time. And price went up to 82k, then back down to 58k, and now trading at around 63k.

During all this time, of course I've reviewed my analysis to see if something was wrong and if price could go lower from here. But, the more I checked, the more it confirmed the bullish bias.

So... to what extent is it healthy to keep checking, to try to control every variable?

In the end, the result is not up to us. Market analysis doesn't give you 100% probabilities, never. There are no guarantees. You can position yourself on the side of probability, and that's what matters. But even more important is knowing how to wait, to have patience. 

And overanalyzing, besides causing unnecessary stress, can make you change your mind simply because what you expect is not happening yet.

The market could remain within a range for more weeks, or it could start going up from here. That's difficult to know. What you need to know is how to not let that affect you while you keep living your life, and how to adapt if something unexpected occurs.

Therefore, the lesson here is trust, acceptance, and detachment. Trust because you've done your best. Acceptance to embrace the reality of the present moment and its timing. And detachment by understanding that the final outcome doesn't fully depend on you. That depends on something much bigger than us.

And this applies to everything in life.

Israel's Democracy: Where Everyone Agrees the Economy Matters and Nobody Votes On It

A new poll just handed Israeli politics its own confession booth, and the testimony is glorious. Ask citizens what's most urgent, and 26.4% across every religious stripe say the economy — the one thing seculars, traditionalists, and the religious actually agree on. Ask what decides their vote, and the economy drops to fourth place at 9.6%. First place, at 30.9%, is "the leader's personality".

So Israelis vote on vibes, then wonder why the cost of living never gets fixed. Democracy, but make it a personality cult.

Speaking of cults: Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu polls at 29.2% overall, yet among voters who think the country's on the right track, 60.9% call him the best man for the job — while only 39.5% of that same happy crowd say they'll actually vote Likud. A 21-point gap between loving the king and voting for his party. Somewhere in there is a man Israelis want on the throne but not on the ballot.

Meanwhile the two camps can't even agree on what country they live in. 42.8% of secular Israelis insist Israel is basically a religious state; 49.8% of religious Israelis insist it's basically secular. Both sides are convinced they're losing the same war — a fight with no finish line, because nobody's actually counting the same scoreboard.

Into this void steps Derech Eretz, running the state's plumbing because the state itself apparently can't read paperwork: the Chief Rabbinate, per the report, still can't process Soviet-era documents, leaving Russian-speaking Israelis waiting years for the kind of marriage and burial approvals other citizens get in a week. The fix on the table — elected neighborhood councils, a Russian-speaking chief rabbi — isn't radical. It's just what happens when volunteers have to build the office the government forgot to open.

Two-thirds of Israelis are dissatisfied with their government. Nine in ten have already made up their minds anyway. If that's not a definition of a stuck system, what is?

If nobody votes on the problem they call urgent, and nobody agrees on what country they're voting for — who exactly is the electorate representing?
